title: The Changing Economic World: The UK Economy

examTip: The UK is a post-industrial HIC: most people work in services. Use named UK examples (Cambridge Science Park, Toyota at Burnaston, HS2, the Outer Hebrides) and judge how much each change matters.
introTips: Know the three causes of economic change: deindustrialisation, globalisation and government policies.
Learn one example of each: a science park, a sustainable factory, a growing and a declining rural area, a transport project.
The north–south divide: know the gap and two strategies to close it.
intro: In the past, many people in Britain worked in coal mines, steelworks and shipyards. Today most work in offices, shops, hospitals and labs. This lesson explains why the UK's economy changed and what the new economy looks like. It also covers its effects on the environment, the countryside and different regions, and the UK's links with the rest of the world.

basics.text: A country's economy is all the work, buying and selling that happens there. It includes farms, factories, shops and offices.
An industry is a type of work that makes goods or services. Coal mining and banking are industries. A factory is a building where goods are made.
Some jobs make things, such as building cars. Other jobs give a service, such as teaching, nursing or working in a shop.
The government runs the country. It decides how to spend public money, such as on roads, trains and schools.

basics.idea: North and south in the UK
basics.text: The south of England includes London and the South East. The north includes cities such as Manchester, Leeds and Newcastle.
Rural means in the countryside, away from towns. Urban means in towns and cities.
Trade is buying and selling between countries. Selling goods to another country is exporting. Buying goods from another country is importing.

keyPoints.heading: Causes of economic change in the UK
keyPoints.content: The UK's economy has changed from making things to providing services. Three causes explain why. Deindustrialisation is the decline of traditional industries such as coal mining, steel, shipbuilding and textiles. Coal and iron ore ran out or became costly to dig, and machines replaced many workers. Globalisation is the way countries have become more connected through trade, travel and communication. Factories in countries with lower wages could make goods more cheaply, so many UK factories closed. Government policies also mattered. Later, governments stopped protecting loss-making industries such as coal, and encouraged service industries such as banking instead. Whole towns built around a mine or a steelworks lost their main employer, and some, in places such as South Yorkshire and South Wales, still have high unemployment.
writeBullets: Deindustrialisation: decline of coal, steel, shipbuilding, textiles; resources ran out, machines replaced workers
Globalisation: goods made more cheaply abroad, so UK factories closed
Government policies: stopped protecting loss-making industries; encouraged services
Legacy: former mining and steel towns lost their main employer

keyTerms.def: The decline of manufacturing and heavy industry in a country, and the loss of the jobs that went with it.
The way countries have become more connected through trade, travel, investment and communication.
The old heavy industries the UK grew rich on, such as coal mining, steel making, shipbuilding and textiles.

keyPoints.memTip: Decline, global, government: three causes of change.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Students often do not know what "traditional industries" are: name them.

keyPoints.heading: Towards a post-industrial economy
keyPoints.content: The UK is now a post-industrial economy: most people work in services, not factories. In 2025 services made up about 73% of the UK's economy, manufacturing about 8% and farming, forestry and fishing under 1%. The UK's GNI per head was $54,550. The growing parts are information technology (software, the internet), finance (banking and insurance, especially in London), other services such as retail and health, and research. Remember the sectors: primary takes raw materials, secondary makes things, tertiary provides services. Work based on knowledge and research is a fourth sector, the quaternary sector. Much of this work happens in science parks and business parks. A science park is a group of research and high-tech companies, usually next to a university, so they can share ideas and hire graduates. A business park is a group of offices and light industry on the edge of a town. Both are usually near main roads or motorways, with space and pleasant surroundings. Cambridge Science Park, beside the University of Cambridge and close to main roads, is home to many technology and medical research companies.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: The shift from making things to providing services.
writeBullets: Post-industrial: most work is in services; services about 73% of the economy, manufacturing about 8% (2025)
Growth: IT, finance, services, research
Quaternary sector: knowledge and research work
Science park: research and high-tech firms next to a university
Business park: offices and light industry on a town's edge
Located near universities, main roads, with space; example: Cambridge Science Park

keyTerms.def: An economy where most people work in services rather than in factories, mining or farming.
Jobs based on knowledge, research and information, such as scientific research and software design.
A group of research and high-tech companies built together, usually next to a university.
A group of offices and light industry built together, usually on the edge of a town near a main road.

keyPoints.memTip: Science parks hug universities; business parks hug ring roads.
keyPoints.tutor_note: On a map, give evidence and say why it helps: a university nearby for ideas and graduates, a main road for access.

keyPoints.heading: Industry and the environment
keyPoints.content: Industry can harm the physical environment. Old mines and steelworks left scarred land, waste heaps and polluted rivers. Factories still use energy, make waste and give off pollution, and new buildings cover green fields. Modern industrial development can be more environmentally sustainable, meaning it does less harm to the environment now and in the future. Toyota's car factory at Burnaston, near Derby, is one example. It aims to run on renewable energy, such as solar and wind power, and to cut its waste. Part of the site has been made into a wildlife reserve with the Derbyshire Wildlife Trust. But no factory is completely green: building it and bringing in materials and workers still uses energy and creates pollution.
writeBullets: Harm: scarred land, waste heaps, polluted rivers, energy use, building on green fields
Sustainable: does less harm now and in the future
Toyota at Burnaston: renewable energy (solar, wind), less waste, on-site wildlife reserve
Limits: building it and transporting materials and workers still pollutes

keyTerms.def: Meeting people's needs today while doing as little harm as possible to the environment, so it stays healthy for the future.
Energy from sources that do not run out, such as the Sun and the wind.

keyPoints.memTip: Sustainable = less harm, now and later.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Explain how each step helps the environment, and say what still harms it.

keyPoints.heading: Change in the countryside
keyPoints.content: The rural landscape is changing in two different ways. In an area of population growth, such as South Cambridgeshire, near Cambridge, people move in because jobs in Cambridge and its science parks are close and transport is good. New housing estates are built, and house prices rise so some local young people cannot afford to buy. Traffic gets busier, but village shops and schools gain customers and pupils. In an area of population decline, such as the Outer Hebrides, islands off north-west Scotland, young people leave to find work and study. The population that stays is older. Shops, schools and bus services close because too few people use them, and there are fewer workers. Tourism and renewable energy, such as wind power, bring some new jobs.
writeBullets: Growth (South Cambridgeshire): people move in near Cambridge's jobs; new estates; higher house prices; more traffic; village services gain
Decline (Outer Hebrides): young people leave; older population; shops, schools, buses close; fewer workers
New chances for declining areas: tourism, renewable energy

keyTerms.def: People, especially the young, leaving the countryside for towns and cities, so the population falls and grows older.

keyPoints.memTip: Near the jobs, villages grow; far from them, they shrink.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Name one area of growth and one of decline, with a social and an economic change for each.

keyPoints.heading: Transport and the north–south divide
keyPoints.content: Better infrastructure, the transport and networks a country needs, can help the economy. Roads: busy motorways and main roads are widened. Rail: HS2, a high-speed line, is being built from London to Birmingham; its planned northern sections were cancelled. Ports: new deep-water container terminals, such as Liverpool2 at the Port of Liverpool, let the biggest ships dock. Airports: Heathrow has plans for a third runway, which are hotly debated. The UK also has a north–south divide: on average, people in London and the South East earn more and live longer than people in much of the north, Wales and Northern Ireland. Much of the post-industrial growth came to the south. Strategies to close the gap include giving more power and money to elected city mayors, such as in Greater Manchester (called devolution), better transport between northern cities, and enterprise zones that offer businesses lower taxes to set up in poorer areas. The gap is still wide.
keyPoints.diagramCaption: How the north compares with the south: a broad pattern, not a hard line.
writeBullets: Roads: busy motorways and main roads widened
Rail: HS2 London to Birmingham; northern sections cancelled
Ports: Liverpool2 deep-water container terminal
Airports: plans for a third runway at Heathrow
North–south divide: on average the south earns more and lives longer
Strategies: devolution to city mayors, better northern transport, enterprise zones; gap still wide

keyTerms.def: The basic networks a country needs to work, such as roads, railways, ports, airports and power lines.
The gap in wealth, health and jobs between the generally richer south-east of England and much of the rest of the UK.
Handing powers and money from the national government to regional or city governments, such as an elected mayor.
An area where the government gives businesses lower taxes and simpler rules to encourage them to set up there.

keyPoints.memTip: Better links, more power to the regions, tax breaks: three ways to close the gap.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Judge each strategy: say what it does and how much it has helped.

keyPoints.heading: The UK's place in the wider world
keyPoints.content: The UK is linked to the rest of the world in many ways. Trade: it buys and sells goods and services worldwide, and London is one of the world's biggest financial centres. Culture: British music, films, television, football and the English language are known around the world. Transport: airports such as Heathrow and ports such as Liverpool and Felixstowe connect it to every continent. Electronic communication: undersea internet cables link the UK to Europe and North America. Economic and political links: the UK left the European Union (EU), a group of European countries that trade freely with each other; trade with the EU now has more checks and paperwork, though the EU is still a major trading partner. The UK is also a member of the Commonwealth, a group of countries, most once ruled by Britain, that work together on trade and development.
writeBullets: Trade: worldwide; London a major financial centre
Culture: music, film, TV, football, the English language
Transport: Heathrow, ports such as Liverpool and Felixstowe
Electronic communication: undersea internet cables
EU: the UK left; more checks on trade, but still a major partner
Commonwealth: countries, mostly once ruled by Britain, working together

keyTerms.def: A group of European countries that trade freely with each other and share some laws. The UK left it.
A group of countries, most of them once ruled by Britain, that work together on trade, development and shared values.

keyPoints.memTip: Trade, culture, transport, cables: four kinds of link; EU and Commonwealth: two clubs.
keyPoints.tutor_note: For a 6-mark answer, explain how a change in a link (leaving the EU) affects the UK's place in the world.

1.question: Why are science parks usually built next to universities?
options: So companies can share research ideas and hire graduates
Because land next to universities is always cheapest
So students can work in the factories at weekends
Because universities must own all science parks
1.correctFeedback: Right. Being near a university gives companies research ideas and skilled graduates to hire.
1.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Science parks are near universities so companies can share research and hire graduates.

3.question: Which is a change in a rural area of population decline, such as the Outer Hebrides?
options: Shops, schools and bus services close as young people leave
New housing estates are built for people moving in
House prices rise because many people want to move in
3.correctFeedback: Right. With fewer, older people, services close because too few use them.
3.wrongFeedback: Not quite. New estates, busier traffic and rising prices happen in areas of growth. In decline, services close as young people leave.

commonMistakes: Not knowing what traditional industries are: coal, steel, shipbuilding and textiles.
Naming map features for a science park site without saying why each one helps.
Saying a factory is sustainable without explaining how each step reduces harm.
Answering rural change in terms of poor countries' problems. Keep to the UK: services closing, house prices, an older population.
Using a vague "jobs and money" answer for transport. Name the project and explain who it helps and how.
Forgetting the Commonwealth when asked about the UK's political links.
examTips: For a science park map question, give a piece of map evidence and why it makes a good site (university nearby, main road, space).
For sustainability, use Toyota at Burnaston: renewable energy, less waste, wildlife reserve, and say what still harms the environment.
For rural change, use one area of growth (South Cambridgeshire) and one of decline (Outer Hebrides).
For transport, name projects (HS2, Liverpool2, Heathrow third runway) and judge their effect on the economy and the north–south divide.
